forces: Orchestra with offstage oboe and four timpanists
intro: A cor anglais calls across the orchestra to a distant oboe: two shepherds at the end of the day. When the call returns, only thunder answers.

cues.title: Two shepherds call
cues.text: A cor anglais and a distant oboe exchange slow phrases. The oboe is marked lontano — far away. There is no accompaniment at first; the shepherds have the orchestra to themselves.
cues.evidence: Movement III, opening bars, Michel Austin’s score transcription: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas3.pdf . Berlioz’s programme identifies the two players as shepherds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three weeks in the countryside
cues.text: This Adagio costs Berlioz more than three weeks of work. He puts it aside and returns to it two or three times. In his Mémoires, he sets that struggle beside the march to the scaffold, which he writes in a single night.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 26, on composing the third and fourth movements: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Flute and violins sing
cues.text: The flute and first violins begin a broad melody in F major, playing together in unison. Plucked strings join beneath them. The shepherds’ short calls have opened onto a song that can stretch across the hillside.
cues.evidence: Movement III, principal theme from bar 20, with plucked string accompaniment joining at bar 24; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 2–3.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An unaccustomed calm
cues.text: In Berlioz’s programme, the evening, the shepherds’ ranz des vaches, trees stirred lightly by the wind and a few new hopes bring the artist “an unaccustomed calm”. He thinks of his isolation, and hopes not to be alone much longer.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s programme, part III, in both the 1845 and 1855 versions (“un calme inaccoutumé”): http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Beethoven’s birdsong
cues.text: F major is the key of Beethoven’s Pastoral Symphony, and this scene is Berlioz’s homage to it. In the pages after the main melody he slips in discreet allusions to the birdsong that closes the Pastoral’s slow movement.
cues.evidence: Michel Austin’s commentary on movement III: the movement recalls the Pastoral Symphony in the same key, with intentional echoes of its bird song from bar 67: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Unease among the trees
cues.text: The middle episode brings shorter wind phrases and increasingly restless strings. The idée fixe enters this troubled countryside in the woodwinds and, reshaped, in the basses. Berlioz’s artist begins to fear that his beloved is deceiving him.
cues.evidence: Movement III, central episode, including the idée fixe at bars 87–102; score and commentary: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm . The fear of betrayal appears in Berlioz’s programme, part III.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet above plucked strings
cues.text: The woodwinds soften as the pastoral music returns. A solo clarinet takes the tune above softly plucked second violins and divided violas. The flute echoes it; the string players keep their bows off the strings.
cues.evidence: Movement III, bars 110–123: Tempo I, quiet woodwind phrases, pizzicato accompaniment and solo clarinet from bar 119. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 21–22.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A melody from the Mass
cues.text: The pastoral tune begins life in the Gratias of Berlioz’s Messe solennelle, written in 1824–25. He moves it from E major to F major for the symphony. The Mass disappears for generations; its rediscovery in 1991 reveals the borrowing.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, composition history and third-movement commentary: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Hiller helps rewrite the scene
cues.text: At the première in December 1830, this movement makes little impression. Berlioz decides to rewrite it. His friend Ferdinand Hiller offers advice, and the long countryside scene takes its place among the revisions Berlioz makes over several years.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31, on the third movement’s reception and Hiller’s advice; chapter 26, on revisions over several years: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Thunder answers the shepherd
cues.text: The cor anglais calls again. The distant oboe stays silent. Four timpanists supply the thunder, their rolls rising and fading beneath the solitary voice. Berlioz asks for soft sponge-headed sticks.
cues.evidence: Movement III, bars 175–196; the score specifies four timpanists and baguettes d’éponge. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 37–38. The unanswered call and thunder are named in the programme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sun goes down
cues.text: Berlioz ends this scene in his 1855 programme with a few broken phrases: “The sun goes down … distant thunder … solitude … silence.” The second shepherd never answers.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, programme of Symphonie fantastique, 1855 version, part III. Our translation of “Le soleil se couche… bruit éloigné du tonnerre… solitude… silence…”: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Next, the opium
cues.text: After the silence, the 1845 programme turns to the artist’s despair. Sure that his love is unrecognised, he takes opium. The dose is too weak to kill him; it brings strange visions, and in them he is led to the scaffold.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 programme, part IV, Marche au supplice (“l’artiste s’empoisonne avec de l’opium”): http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

transitions.title: The flute opens a longer phrase
transitions.from: Intro · Cor anglais and distant oboe
transitions.to: A · Flute and violins in F
transitions.how: The shepherds’ exchange ends. Flute and first violins begin the principal tune in F major, in unison and almost alone. Plucked second violins, violas, cellos and basses join beneath the melody. The broad Adagio continues.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 20–28; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 2–3.

transitions.title: The pastoral tune breaks into fragments
transitions.from: A · Flute and violins in F
transitions.to: B · The beloved disturbs the countryside
transitions.how: The F-major pastoral tune gives way to short wind phrases. Strings begin to climb, adding chromatic notes and repeated figures; bassoons, cellos and basses will take a distorted form of the idée fixe beneath trembling violin chords. The score marks the gathering string figures crescendo poco a poco.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, approach to the central episode and bars 81–102, especially the crescendo at bar 83 and bass-line idée fixe from bar 87; Michel Austin’s score transcription.

transitions.title: The strings put down their bows
transitions.from: B · The beloved disturbs the countryside
transitions.how: The agitated phrases slow and fade. At Tempo I, flute and oboes answer a sustained note in the solo cellos. The return of the pastoral tune brings a new accompaniment: plucked semiquavers in second violins and divided violas, marked pianississimo, beneath a solo clarinet.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 110–123, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 21–22: rallentando, Tempo I, solo cellos and pizzicato accompaniment.

transitions.title: The oboe leaves the shepherd alone
transitions.how: The F-major pastoral music thins to plucked strings and quiet wind chords. At un poco ritenuto, it yields to the cor anglais. The opening call returns without the distant oboe; timpani tuned to B♭, F, A♭ and C roll beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 171–182, Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 37; the timpani parts specify the four pitches.

source.title: Berlioz, Scène aux champs — orchestral score
source.locator: Shepherds’ calls, bars 1–20; pastoral theme from bar 20; central idée fixe, bars 87–102; returning call and thunder, bars 175–196; final string chords, bars 197–199.

timeline.note: Cor anglais and distant oboe exchange unaccompanied calls.
Muted, divided violas join the shepherds’ calls.
Flute and first violins sing the pastoral tune; plucked strings join beneath them.
Woodwinds and strings exchange the pastoral tune and its accompanying figures.
Short wind phrases lead into climbing string figures and the central idée fixe.
Quiet woodwind phrases give way to a solo clarinet above plucked second violins and violas.
The cor anglais calls alone; four timpanists answer with distant thunder.
The cor anglais continues between soft, overlapping timpani rolls.
The thunder fades; quiet horns and bowed strings close in F major.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and announced that he was tired, allowing the boy to escape without having to explain his tears. Berlioz remembered the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt flute and guitar, pored over maps of distant islands and took Virgil’s abandoned queen personally.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
